name: NoisyTCP
tile_line: Remote crash of Linux servers; patch if TCP is exposed.
summary: NoisyTCP (CVE-2026-99288) is an 11-year-old race in the Linux kernel's TCP code that lets anyone who can reach a listening TCP port crash the whole server, with no login; its finder, Hyunwoo Kim, crashed default Nginx, Apache and SSH servers on virtual machines in about 5 seconds to 2 minutes, while a quiet physical server took about 14 hours. He says it isn't practically remote code execution yet and his exploit isn't public; fixes are out for Debian and the current RHEL 8, 9 and 10 releases, and on the way for Ubuntu. Its sibling from the same patch series, the [Linux 9.8 race](/linux-socket-race/), only matters on weakly ordered processors such as Arm and POWER and has its own fixes, so a kernel fixed for NoisyTCP isn't necessarily fixed for it.

affected.label: Kernel 4.4 or later, unpatched
affected.text: The bug came in with a 2015 change in kernel 4.4. Upstream fixed it in 5.10.275, 5.15.226, 6.1.193, 6.6.163, 6.12.117, 6.18.63, 7.3.4 and 7.4-rc2. Red Hat says RHEL 6 and 7 are not affected. Distro kernels backport, so compare with your distro's version under Update.

affected.label: A TCP port the attacker can reach
affected.text: Any service that listens on TCP, such as Nginx, Apache or SSH in their default setup, with no login needed. The attack uses SYN cookies, which Kim says are on by default on most distributions. If the service runs in a container, the whole host goes down, not just the container.

affected.label: Packets spread across several CPUs
affected.text: Kim says the race needs packets handled concurrently on different CPUs. That's possible when the interface the attacker's traffic arrives on has two or more receive queues, or when RPS (receive packet steering) is turned on for it. The command is a first check: it prints one line per receive queue with its RPS setting. One `rx-` line for that interface and a setting of all zeros (RPS's default) means you don't meet this condition. More lines, or a non-zero setting, means packets can be spread out; whether they actually land on different CPUs depends on which CPUs each queue's interrupt and the RPS setting point to.

do.label: Update the kernel and reboot
do.text: Fixed in the current releases: Debian 12 6.1.192-1, Debian 13 6.12.117-1, RHEL 8 4.18.0-553.189.1.el8_10, RHEL 9.9 5.14.0-741.26.1.el9_9 and RHEL 10.3 6.12.0-264.19.1.el10_3. Older RHEL update streams (such as 8.8, 9.8 and 10.2) have no fixed kernel yet. Ubuntu lists fixes in progress for its main kernel on every release from 16.04 to 26.10; most of its other kernels (cloud, HWE, Raspberry Pi and others) are still listed as vulnerable on the releases they ship for, with no fix in progress yet. On Arm and POWER, a netdev review bot asked for this fix to be backported together with the [Linux 9.8 race](/linux-socket-race/) fix, because without it the crash might still be reachable there; no maintainer has confirmed that, and older stable kernels (5.10 to 6.6) have only this fix so far.

do.label: Can't update yet? Two stopgaps
do.text: Both come from Kim and Red Hat. Turn SYN cookies off by setting `net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies` to 0; it blocks the SYN cookie path the crash uses, has to be set in each network namespace (so in each container too), and weakens protection against SYN floods. Or cut the receive queues of the internet-facing interface to one and turn RPS and RFS off.

do.label: Why it isn't Patch now
do.text: The easy path only crashes servers: Red Hat says it "does not allow data alteration or arbitrary code execution", and the kernel CVE team scores no data impact. Kim calls it remote corruption and describes a second, much harder path that can reach freed memory, which kernel maintainer Eric Dumazet disputed when the fix was first posted. On code execution Kim says "Not yet. and basically, no": he has only "a very limited, lab-specific exploit that targets VM servers", and his GitHub page has no exploit code. No attacks are reported and it isn't on CISA's list of exploited bugs. Ratings differ: the kernel CVE team gives 7.5, Ubuntu High, Red Hat Important (its 7.5 vector assumes an attacker with some privileges who can read and change data, which its own statement rules out), and CISA's entry in the CVE record 5.9, rating the timing hard. We'd change the verdict to Patch now if working exploit code is published or attacks are reported.

slack: NoisyTCP (CVE-2026-99288), Linux kernel, write-up published 15 Nov 2026: a TCP race that lets anyone who can reach a listening TCP port crash the whole server, no login, default configs (Nginx, Apache, SSH). Needs two or more receive queues or RPS. The finder crashed VMs in 5 s to 2 min; a quiet physical server took 14 h. The easy path only crashes the host; the finder says it isn't practically RCE yet; his exploit isn't public; no attacks, not on CISA KEV. Fixed: Debian 12 6.1.192-1, Debian 13 6.12.117-1, RHEL 8, 9.9, 10.3; Ubuntu in progress; older RHEL 9.x and 10.x streams not yet. Stopgaps: SYN cookies off (net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=0, per namespace) or a single receive queue with RPS/RFS off.
